The authors performed thin-sample directional solidification experiments on a transparent CBr4-1.4 mol% C2Cl6 alloy with a thermal gradient of 120 ± 20 K/cm.
The nominal constitutional supercooling and Mullins-Sekerka threshold velocities for this alloy composition are V_CS ≈ 15 μm/s and V_MS ≈ 20 μm/s, respectively.
For solidification velocities V < 6 μm/s, the solid-liquid interface remained planar across the entire sample width, with subboundary grooves having a depth comparable to the equilibrium state.
In the velocity range 6-10 μm/s, the authors observed a pre-cellulation of the interface near grain boundary grooves, as predicted by the theory of Coriell and Sekerka.
Fully developed cellular patterns were observed for solidification velocities greater than 15 ± 4 μm/s.
The phase-field simulations used a grand-canonical multi-phase-field formulation with three phase fields representing the two solid grains and the liquid.
The grain boundary energy anisotropy was modeled using a smooth, cusp-like function with deep but smooth minima to avoid numerical issues.
The ratio of the capillary length d_0 to the interface thickness parameter ε was fixed at 1.58 in the simulations.
The temperature gradient G was chosen such that the thermal diffusion length l_T was 100 times the capillary length d_0.
The authors implemented a regularization technique by adding the square of the Laplacian of each phase field to the free energy functional, with a prefactor β.
